Series::besselk¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signatures¶

Series Series::besselk() const
Series Series::besselk(double order) const

The Decaying Modified Bessel Family¶

besselk() evaluates the modified Bessel function of the second kind, K_order(x), elementwise. It solves the same modified Bessel equation as besseli(), but chooses the independent solution that decays exponentially for positive x. This is the branch used for radial effects that must vanish with distance rather than grow.

The no-argument form means order zero. The overload accepts one finite real order shared by every lane. K_v is even in its order: K_-v(x) = K_v(x). Its real-valued domain is the positive axis. At zero it has a positive singularity and returns inf; negative arguments return NaN lane by lane. Those values describe the mathematical boundary. A non-finite order is instead a malformed call and raises an exception.

The operation allocates a shape-preserving floating result. Integral input is promoted to float64; the receiver is not modified. The positive-real kernel uses a stable integral representation, avoiding the nearly singular sin(pi*order) quotient that loses precision close to integer orders.

Reverse Mode¶

The derivative is negative one half of the adjacent-order sum:

d K_v(x) / dx = -(K_(v-1)(x) + K_(v+1)(x)) / 2

For order zero, this becomes -K_1(x), matching the fact that K_0 decreases on the positive axis.

Examples¶

Example 1. The default order decays rapidly as the argument grows.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0}).besselk());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.9244, 0.4210, 0.1139, 0.0112]

Example 2. Order one is a distinct member of the same decaying family.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0}).besselk(1.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1.6564, 0.6019, 0.1399, 0.0125]

Example 3. Domain outcomes are carried independently for each lane.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-1.0, 0.0, 1.0}).besselk());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[nan, inf, 0.4210]

Example 4. Reverse mode for K_0 produces the negative K_1 values.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.besselk().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.6564, -0.6019, -0.1399]

Example 5. Order sign does not change the result.

const auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.0, 2.0});
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << x.besselk(-1.5).allclose(x.besselk(1.5)) << "\n";

Output¶

true

See Also¶

  • besseli() is finite at zero and grows on the positive axis.

  • bessely() is the singular oscillatory second solution.
